rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to test which critical pairs respond to slope. This comparison will guide window trimming and distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from pairs requiring temperature changes.
Keep the shallower gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity at the remaining overlap. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, potentially removing the time penalty.

Back off from 60 C to separate the newly co-eluting pair, while retaining much of the temperature-driven selectivity improvement. Shortening the gradient slightly should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.
Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the remaining critical pair while preserving the favorable selectivity at 55 C. The last peak should remain near, but below, 10 minutes.

The remaining pair at 55 C responds weakly to slope but was better separated at 60 C. Test a steeper gradient at 60 C to move the later co-eluting pair away from its crossover while keeping the run comfortably below 10 minutes.
Make a small slope reduction to lift the R = 1.46 pair toward full resolution. This tests whether it reaches 1.5 before the later R = 1.64 pair loses full credit, with ample margin below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient beyond the later pair's co-elution crossover, rather than balancing two opposing resolution limits near injection 6. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the longer gradient and help keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Shift the starting composition upward while slightly flattening the gradient to adjust the balance between the two critical pairs. This tests a nearby solvent-window change rather than slope alone, while keeping retention comfortably below 10 minutes.

Use the narrower programmed window to obtain a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, just steeper than injection 9. This small adjustment should raise the R = 1.49 pair above 1.5 while preserving the other critical separations; all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Injection 10 already achieves the maximum CRF; now test whether a higher starting organic fraction can shorten the fully resolved separation. A compensating shallower slope should help preserve the early critical pairs, while testing the resolution limit of the later pair.

Return to the fully resolved starting composition and increase the slope only slightly, from 0.045 to 0.04583 per minute. This should shorten the separation while testing whether the narrow resolution margins of injection 10 remain above 1.5.

Injection 10 retains the maximum score, and the local slope increase has reached a resolution limit. Explore a cooler selectivity regime with a higher starting organic fraction to seek another fully resolved method without excessive retention.

Hold the gradient fixed and lower temperature to test whether the two overlaps at 35 C separate in the cooler selectivity regime. The current retention window leaves some room for the expected increase in retention before a time penalty applies.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 25 C to improve the lone R = 1.40 pair and establish a second fully resolved selectivity regime. The last peak is expected to remain close to 10 minutes; injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction and shorten the gradient to reduce retention in the fully resolved 25 C regime. The slope remains close to injection 15, whose minimum resolution of 1.89 provides some margin for compression.

Lengthen the gradient one step to recover the critical separation lost at the higher starting composition. This tests whether full resolution can be restored while keeping the last peak earlier than in injection 15.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the cool-temperature separation, compensating with a shallower gradient to protect the critical pair. Injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Explore the shallower-slope side of the late-pair crossover at 60 C, using a higher starting organic fraction to limit retention. This may provide a second high-temperature route to full resolution with more separation margin than injection 10.

Test the intermediate cool-temperature selectivity at 30 C using injection 16's gradient. A modest temperature increase may improve its lone critical pair while shortening retention, without reaching the overlaps observed at 35 C.

At 30 C, test a higher starting composition with a shallower slope to rebalance the two adjacent critical pairs. The higher start should offset some of the retention increase from flattening the gradient; injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Lengthen injection 21's gradient one step to improve the remaining R = 1.26 overlap. Monitor the final pair, currently at R = 1.72, for loss of resolution as the slope decreases; retention should remain below 10 minutes.

Refine injection 18 by lengthening its gradient one step, aiming to raise the lone R = 1.33 pair above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This could establish another maximum-score method; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved option.

Slightly flatten injection 17's gradient to increase its narrow R = 1.52 margin while aiming to retain full resolution below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a more forgiving alternative to the faster injection 10.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 24 to seek greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak just below 10 minutes. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method; this final run tests a more forgiving alternative.
